analysis.one_liner: Terminates federal price support programs for sugar beets and sugarcane.
analysis.headline: The bill, which had no cosponsors, was referred to the House Agriculture Committee and its specialty crops subcommittee in July 1999 and never received a hearing, vote, or further action before the 106th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The federal government runs a sugar price support program: it guarantees a minimum price for sugar beets and sugarcane through government loans and purchases, which keeps domestic sugar prices well above world levels. This bill would repeal that program outright, ending the guaranteed price floor for the 2000 and later crops while settling any loans already made. It would save taxpayers money on any defaults and lower the cost of sugar in food, but it would remove a safety net that sugar growers have relied on for decades.
analysis.who_benefits: Households and food manufacturers who buy sugar would gain if the repeal pushed retail sugar prices down, since price supports hold domestic sugar prices above world market levels. Taxpayers would also be spared the cost when growers default on government sugar loans. Importantly, the bill only repeals the price support program; it does not touch the import quotas that separately restrict sugar entering the country, so the savings for shoppers would be smaller than full sugar program reform.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals Section 156 of the Agricultural Market Transition Act, which is the sugarcane and sugar beet price support program, and bars the Agriculture Department from providing any further price support for those crops through loans, payments, or purchases.

Repealing price supports would remove the government-guaranteed price floor that keeps domestic sugar prices above what they would be otherwise, which is a cost consumers pay at the grocery store every time they buy sweetened foods.
The bill takes effect October 1, 1999, and applies to the 2000 and subsequent crops, while requiring the government to settle loans already outstanding so no existing obligation is wiped out.

analysis.who_pays: Sugar beet and sugarcane growers and the processors who mill their crops would lose the guaranteed minimum price and the government loan safety net, exposing them to price swings and, in bad years, selling at prices below their cost of production. Sugar-producing regions, concentrated in states like Florida, Louisiana, Minnesota, and North Dakota, would bear the economic adjustment.

drawbacks.text: The bill repeals price support but leaves sugar import quotas untouched, so the domestic sugar supply would remain artificially restricted and the price savings for consumers would be far smaller than they would be under full sugar program reform.

Growers would lose a decades-old safety net without any transition assistance. In years of low prices or oversupply, beet and cane farmers could face losses that the loan program previously cushioned, which is the strongest good-faith argument for keeping supports in place.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill went after the part of the sugar program that costs consumers and taxpayers, but only half of it. Repealing price supports would deliver real savings to shoppers and spare taxpayers from loan defaults, yet because it leaves the sugar import quota system in place, the market would still be tightly restricted and prices would stay well above world levels. Growers would absorb real risk with no phase-out or transition aid. A better-designed bill would have paired repeal with transition help and taken on the quotas as well.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Agriculture Committee and then to its specialty crops subcommittee in July 1999, and no one ever took it up for a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. David Wu introduced the bill in the House on July 22, 1999.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Agriculture, and five days later to the Subcommittee on Risk Management, Research and Specialty Crops.
No hearing, markup, floor vote, or further action of any kind followed; the bill's action history ends with the subcommittee referral, and it died when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.
The bill attracted zero cosponsors in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Sugar beet and sugarcane growers and processors are better off, because the government price guarantee they rely on survived untouched. Consumers and taxpayers, who pay for the program through higher sugar prices and loan losses, are no better off than before.

for.name: Rep. David Wu
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the sugar price support program; it drew no cosponsors.

against.name: House Agriculture Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to committee and subcommittee and never scheduled a hearing or markup, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Sugar beet and sugarcane growers and processors
against.role: Producers protected by the federal sugar price support program
against.what_they_did: The sugar industry has long organized to defend the federal sugar program, and no member of Congress from sugar-producing districts joined this repeal effort.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no roll calls exist; its single sponsor was a Democrat and it attracted no cosponsors of either party, and Agriculture Committee members of both parties generally defend commodity support programs.

industries.note: The bill would have ended their guaranteed price floor and government loan safety net, exposing them to market prices. Keeping price supports in place keeps a cost on ordinary people, since the guaranteed price is paid by shoppers in the form of sugar prices held above world levels.
Processors operate the loan program and buy beets and cane under the supported price structure; repeal would have removed the financial backing the program provides.
Repeal of the price floor would have pushed sugar prices somewhat lower, cutting costs for anyone who buys sweetened products, though import quotas would have limited the savings.
